summary:
Same-sex conduct is decriminalised in Belize. On 10 August 2016 the Supreme Court, presided over by Chief Justice Kenneth Benjamin, declared Section 53 of the Criminal Code unconstitutional. The challenge was filed in 2010 by LGBT advocate Caleb Orozco and heard in Belize City in May 2013. The Human Dignity Trust documents the case among constitutional challenges to criminalisation statutes in the Eastern Caribbean, and Belize was the first former British Caribbean territory to strike down such a law.

On 30 December 2019 the Court of Appeal upheld the ruling and confirmed that the Constitution's protections against discrimination extend to sexual orientation and that freedom of expression encompasses sexual expression. A visitor faces no criminal exposure for consensual same-sex conduct.

The government did not rest on the ruling. It announced on 17 August 2016 that it would not appeal, then reversed that position after meeting religious leaders on 9 September and filed a partial appeal against the declaration that the Constitution bars discrimination based on sexual orientation. The Catholic Church withdrew from the appeal in March 2018, leaving the government as sole appellant. Solicitor General Nigel Hawke argued that the ruling was judicial overreach in re-defining "sex" to include sexual orientation.

Immigration law is where exposure remains. Section 5(1)(e) of the Immigration Act lists "any prostitute or homosexual" among prohibited immigrants. Jamaican activist Maurice Tomlinson filed a challenge in 2013; the Caribbean Court of Justice granted leave in May 2014, and CARICOM joined as an interested party in October 2014. On 10 June 2016 the CCJ dismissed his case, finding no violation of his freedom of movement. In the litigation Belize contended that Section 5(1) of the Immigration Act applies only to those offering sexual services for financial gain, and that it does not interpret or enforce the act as a blanket prohibition against homosexual immigrants. The CCJ's judgment clarified that neither Belize nor Trinidad and Tobago can ban homosexuals from CARICOM countries from entering, by reason of their obligations under the Treaty of Chaguaramas, notwithstanding the entry bans in their own laws.

Two 2024 statutes name protected grounds. The Anti-Sexual Harassment Act 2024 expressly provides prevention and protection from sexual harassment regardless of sexual preference and gender identity. Section 8(1)(c)(i) of the Alternative Sentencing Act 2024, effective 27 April 2024, makes evidence that an offence was motivated by bias, prejudice or hate based on sexual orientation an aggravating circumstance. The sentencing provision names sexual orientation but not gender identity, while the harassment act names both.

In its 2018 Universal Periodic Review Belize accepted 15 of 17 recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity, the most accepted by any CARICOM country at that review, pledging legal reform, explicit anti-discrimination legislation, police training and SOGI data collection; two recommendations concerning rights equality were noted rather than accepted. Accepted recommendations included concrete steps to ensure universal access to HIV treatment for LGBT people, and training for police officials to respond properly to discrimination, violence and hate crimes against LGBT people.

Belize held its first Pride Week in August 2017, with awareness and acceptance activities hosted around the country, and LGBT organisations have become more visible and active since the 2016 ruling. A 2013 UNAIDS survey of 773 Belizeans aged 18 to 64 found 34 per cent accepting and 34 per cent tolerant of homosexuals, among the highest acceptance rates recorded in the Caribbean in that polling.

The 2013 Supreme Court hearing took place amid violence and death threats received by LGBT activists. Religious bodies were openly hostile: the Council of Churches held a "Take a Stand" rally on 3 December 2011 and a "Belize Action/Family Forum" rally on 23 November 2011 that described decriminalisation as "an orchestrated plan of demonic darkness". In December 2011 Prime Minister Dean Barrow publicly rejected pressure from President Obama, saying Belize would not change its laws. A 1998 protest against a gay cruise ship docking shows that organised hostility to visible LGBT presence predates the litigation.
tangentialFactors:
Belize's 2016 ruling is one strand in the Human Dignity Trust's documentation of constitutional challenges to criminalisation statutes across the Eastern Caribbean, so the litigation route that produced it is a regional pattern rather than a Belize-only event.

The 10 June 2016 Caribbean Court of Justice judgment covered Belize and Trinidad and Tobago together. It grounded the entry question in obligations under the Treaty of Chaguaramas rather than in either state's immigration statute, and both statutes remain on the books.

Belize was the first former British Caribbean territory to overturn its anti-sodomy law.

At the 2018 Universal Periodic Review Belize accepted more sexual orientation and gender identity recommendations than any other CARICOM country in that cycle. The 2013 UNAIDS polling placed it among the highest acceptance rates recorded in the Caribbean.
localsOnly:
The Anti-Sexual Harassment Act 2024 and the Alternative Sentencing Act 2024 govern domestic conduct. Harassment protection applies regardless of sexual preference and gender identity, and a court sentencing an offender must treat bias, prejudice or hate based on sexual orientation as an aggravating circumstance. The aggravating provision does not name gender identity.

Anti-discrimination legislation, police training, SOGI data collection and universal access to HIV treatment for LGBT people were the commitments Belize accepted at the 2018 Universal Periodic Review. The sources consulted record the pledges; they carry no compliance reporting.

Domestic organising has become more visible since 2016, with Pride Week held for the first time in August 2017 and awareness and acceptance activities hosted throughout the country.

Adult attitudes measured in 2013 were split evenly between acceptance and tolerance, with 34 per cent accepting and 34 per cent tolerant among the 773 Belizeans aged 18 to 64 surveyed.
outOfScopeNotes:
No youth- or minor-specific care, medication or travel findings were identified.

No Belize-specific prison practice is sourced. Whether trans detainees are housed by birth sex or by identity, what strip-search rules apply and whether protective segregation is used are unresolved; the only Belize reference in the material on LGBTQ prisoners reviewed here is a navigational taxonomy link.

No documented airport screening or document-marker practice differential to trans travellers is sourced for Belize. Whether a visitor whose documents or presentation differ from recorded details faces secondary screening or anatomy inspection is not established.

Whether Section 5(1)(e) of the Immigration Act has been applied to a trans traveller, and how the act is enforced in practice at ports of entry, is not established by the sources consulted. Belize's position in the Tomlinson litigation is a statement of interpretation, not an account of enforcement.

No data on how Section 8(1)(c)(i) of the Alternative Sentencing Act 2024 has been applied, whether any prosecution has relied on it, or whether gender identity is read into it is available. No trans-specific violence figures with a denominator were identified.
